registers.name: Emotional
registers.desc: Speaking AS the brand. Confident, direct, peer-to-peer, crescendo cadence (short punch, then build). Carries a claim, position, or promise.

registers.name: Receipts
registers.desc: Proof FOR the brand. Cold fact, specifically named, sourced or dated. Numbers, credentials, signed partnerships.

registers.name: Informational
registers.desc: Reporting ABOUT the brand. Plain, third-person, factual. Documents how something works.

note: A post can mix registers, but each sentence should know which one it is in. When precision and voice conflict on an earned brand phrase, voice wins; do not strip an earned phrase to pass a literal slop check.
verbatim:
Where the brand speaks.
Two voices and a third register run through every Disruption Now surface. The brand speaks on some of them. Receipts earn the claim on others. A documentarian reports on the rest. This guide names which register belongs where, and how to tell the difference when you write a new line.
Section 1
What is the line doing?
Every line of brand prose is doing one of three jobs.
Read any line of Disruption Now copy. The line is doing one of three jobs. Speaking AS the brand (emotional). Offering proof FOR the brand (receipts). Reporting structure ABOUT the brand (informational).
01
Speaking AS the brand.
Emotional
The voice is confident, direct, peer-to-peer, with a crescendo cadence (short punch, then build). The line carries a claim, a position, or a promise.
02
Offering proof FOR the brand.
Receipts
The line is cold fact. Specifically named. Sourced or dated. Numbers, credentials, signed partnerships, cited episodes do the work. Receipts earn the claims the brand makes elsewhere.
03
Reporting structure ABOUT the brand.
Informational
The voice is plain, third-person, factual. The line documents how something works, names a relationship, or guides the reader through the chapter.
Sometimes more than one share a paragraph. A documentarian intros the section. The brand speaks in the next breath. A receipt closes the paragraph. The page holds all three.
Section 2
Where the brand speaks.
Every surface listed below carries a claim, a position, or a promise. The brand voice runs through them.
The first words a reader sees on a brand chapter.
On /brand/disruption-now, /brand/midwestcon, /brand/rob-richardson, and the brand-claim-and-principles guide, the top of the page is where the brand introduces itself. The voice carries from the first word.
The brand claim.
One sentence. "We make AI and emerging tech accessible & human-centric." Every deck answers to it. Every page answers to it. Every brand decision answers to it.
Each tagline.
Each brand has one. Disruption Now's is "Making emerging tech accessible & human-centric." A tagline is a single phrase a reader could quote back to you.
The mission line.
A mission line says WHY a brand exists. Disruption Now's opens with "AI is rewriting every industry, but it wasn't built for everyone." The first clause says AI is rewriting every industry. The second says who it leaves out.
The purpose blocks on the Disruption Now chapter.
Eight blocks under §Purpose (tagline, mission, reason, promise, why-we're-different, what-we-stand-for, how-we-work-inside, vision). Each block is a small statement of conviction.
The personas.
"The tech-savvy coworker." "The host who's also your coach." "The disruptor who became the coach." Each persona evokes a character.
Rob's signature lines.
"No one gets to define you." "Coach, not consultant." "From AI consumers to AI producers." Each line is the brand under pressure, compressed.
The phrases the brand has earned.
"Mission made physical." "The people tech overlooks." Three or four words doing the work of a paragraph. The compression carries the brand voice.
Section 3
Where the brand proves.
Receipts. Specific. Named. Sourced. Cold facts that create belief.
The brand voice guardrail names the rule. Every claim needs a receipt, a stat with a source, a story with a name, a number with a date. Receipts are cold facts. They earn the claim through specificity.
Footprint stats.
"741 attendees from 347 organizations across 18-plus states in 2025." "120 AI certifications and $1M+ in documented opportunities, same event." "190+ podcast episodes, 1,000+ monthly listeners, 150+ guests." Each number is specific, dated, sourced.
Founder credentials.
Rob Richardson's record: electrical engineer + lawyer (both UC), youngest UC board chairman, founder of the 1819 Innovation Hub, 2018 Ohio Treasurer candidate with 2M+ votes, civic AI lead on the mayor's Ascend 2030 responsible-AI work. Each credential is a named, verifiable fact that earns Rob's position as the brand's public face.
Documented partnerships and named operations.
Big Kitty Labs as the build partner. Anthropic + Google AI certifications. The 1819 Innovation Hub as the host. UC as the birthplace of cooperative education. Each named operation is on the record.
Specific signature events.
The Disruptors Dinner. The Policy Innovation Lunch. EmpowerHer. Builders & Backers. Up for Debate. Artistic Intelligence. The Disruptors Awards. Each event has a name, a year, attendees, and a documented purpose.
Cited episodes, signed partnerships, deployed workflows.
Every time the brand claims a piece of work, the receipt is the named artifact. "The signed partnership, the published episode, the deployed AI workflow." (Brand voice doc §teamBehavior.)
Receipts are cold facts. They sit in their own register because the job here is to make the reader believe.
Section 4
Where the brand reports.
Plain, grounded, third-person prose. A documentarian writes here. The brand voice steps back.
Architecture matrix cells.
The matrix on /guide/basics/brand-architecture uses one-line cells to cross-reference who-leads-who-endorses-what across DN, MWC, Rob, and BKL. Each cell is a quick tag. Long emotional prose in a matrix cell would break the format.
The pages that explain how something works.
The 90-day path days breakdown. The four streams in practice. The composition primer. Each section tells the reader how a piece of the brand operates.
Status cards.
The architecture chapter has a "brand claim: live and maturing" card that comments on the claim's status. The CARD is a status note. The CLAIM ITSELF lives on the foundation page, where it speaks.
The other voice pages.
/brand/voice/mechanics, /brand/voice/the-gate, /brand/voice/say-this-not-that, /brand/voice/anti-slop-catalog. Each page explains a piece of the voice in plain prose. Their examples quote the brand voice itself.
Footnotes, breadcrumbs, page descriptions, page metadata.
Wayfinding and meta information. Plain by design.
Section 5
Where both share the page.
Some paragraphs run a documentarian's intro into a brand line in the same breath.
The architecture intro paragraph on /guide/basics/brand-architecture is an example. The opening sentence names what the chapter documents (informational). The next sentences describe the three brands, with the brand voice in specific spots. The mixed register works when each sentence knows which voice it is in.
The internal team value names follow the same pattern. Each name is short. The verb carries light brand voice. The qualifier names the audience or the method. Example: "Empowering through applied learning, especially the people tech overlooks." The verb (empowering) and the audience phrasing (the people tech overlooks) are brand voice. The mechanism (applied learning) is one of the brand's frameworks. The whole value name reads as a small operating principle.
Section 6
How to tell which register your line needs.
Three questions before you write.
01
What is this surface for?
If it speaks AS the brand (hero, claim, mission, promise, signature line), the register is emotional. If it offers proof for the claim (stats, credentials, named operations, dated events), the register is receipts. If it documents the brand for reference (matrix, mechanics, status card, breadcrumbs), the register is informational. If more than one belongs on the surface, the register is mixed, and each sentence picks a side.
02
Who is the reader expecting on this surface?
A reader on the foundation page expects to hear from Disruption Now itself. A reader on the brand architecture matrix expects to look up a fact. A reader on the MidwestCon footprint expects numbers that prove the work. Match the voice to the reader's expectation.
03
Could a reader who knows the brand recognize the line as ours?
If yes, the line is brand voice. Replacing it with a literal alternative would strip the recognition. If no, the line is a receipt or a reference, and clarity is the goal.
When the register is unclear, take the line to /brand/voice/the-gate.
Section 7
When emotional gets dulled.
A short worked example.
"Mission made physical" is the canonical MidwestCon framing. Three words. They carry the architectural relationship (MidwestCon is Disruption Now's mission), the mechanism (the mission becomes something physical), and the cadence implied (once a year). The phrase is brand voice.
A check against the voice rules, run alone, can pattern-match "made physical" as abstraction and propose a literal replacement, like "the mission run as a four-day conference." The replacement is procedurally cleaner. The voice is stripped from the line. The substance is preserved.
A phrase that recurs across surfaces, one a reader who knows the brand can quote back, is brand voice. A literal replacement strips it for marginal gain. When the choice is precision against voice, voice wins.
